blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — interpret coagulation test patterns and recognize when focused evaluation is required
stem: A client who is not taking anticoagulants has a prolonged prothrombin time (PT), while the aPTT and platelet count are within reference limits. Which interpretation is most appropriate?

options.A: The normal platelet count makes a quantitative platelet disorder less likely, but the isolated PT result is best interpreted as a platelet-function problem until bleeding symptoms appear.
options.B: The normal aPTT makes intrinsic-pathway deficiencies less likely, so the isolated PT result is most consistent with factor VII deficiency and usually does not require evaluation for acquired causes.
options.C: The normal aPTT and platelet count make vitamin K deficiency and liver disease unlikely, so observation and later repeat PT are preferable to a focused coagulation evaluation.
options.D: The pattern can reflect factor VII deficiency or inhibitor and acquired causes such as vitamin K deficiency or liver disease, so the underlying cause still requires focused evaluation.

rationale: ARUP Consult's current table of PT, aPTT, and platelet-count patterns lists prolonged PT with normal aPTT and normal platelets as a pattern associated with factor VII deficiency or inhibitor and, in some cases, acquired causes including vitamin K deficiency and liver disease. ARUP also states that prolonged clotting times of uncertain etiology require further evaluation. Therefore D is correct. A is incorrect because qualitative platelet disorders are listed among causes that may have normal PT and aPTT; they do not explain this isolated PT pattern simply because the platelet count is normal. B correctly notes that intrinsic-pathway factor VIII or IX deficiencies are a poor fit for isolated PT prolongation, but it incorrectly narrows the result to factor VII and dismisses acquired causes that ARUP explicitly includes. C incorrectly treats vitamin K deficiency and liver disease as poor fits; ARUP lists both among possible causes of prolonged PT with normal aPTT and platelets.
educational_objective: Interpret an isolated prolonged PT with normal aPTT and platelet count as a pattern that narrows the differential toward factor VII deficiency/inhibitor and certain acquired causes, while recognizing that the laboratory pattern requires focused evaluation rather than establishing one diagnosis.
source_version_date: Last Literature Review July 2020; Last Update December 2025; live page retrieved 2026-08-26
source_locator: Laboratory Testing > Condition-Specific Testing > table 'PT, aPTT, and Platelet Count Results and Associated Causes,' row ↑ PT / N aPTT / N platelet count: FVII deficiency or inhibitor; in some cases warfarin, vitamin K deficiency, liver disease, DIC, or oral direct Xa inhibitors. Indications for Testing: prolonged clotting time of uncertain cause should undergo further evaluation.
source_claim_supported: With anticoagulant use excluded in the stem, isolated PT prolongation with normal aPTT and platelet count still has a differential including factor VII deficiency/inhibitor and acquired causes such as vitamin K deficiency and liver disease; further evaluation is needed to identify the cause.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Reduction of Risk Potential, printed p.13/PDF p.17: perform focused assessments; recognize trends and changes in client condition and intervene as needed; monitor the results of diagnostic testing and intervene as needed.
correction_summary: Rebuilt all four alternatives to remove the correct-answer length cue and to keep each option within the same coagulation-interpretation construct. The revised key preserves ARUP's differential wording and does not convert an isolated PT pattern into a single diagnosis.

audit_findings.clinical_category: Hemostasis — interpretation of isolated prolonged PT
audit_findings.stem: PASS — specifies the PT/aPTT/platelet pattern and excludes anticoagulant use without adding assumptions that force a single etiology.
audit_findings.option_A: PASS as distractor — normal platelet count does make a quantitative platelet disorder less likely, but a qualitative platelet disorder does not explain isolated PT prolongation merely on that basis.
audit_findings.option_B: PASS as distractor — intrinsic-pathway deficiencies are a poor fit for isolated PT prolongation, but the result cannot be narrowed to factor VII while dismissing acquired causes listed by ARUP.
audit_findings.option_C: PASS as distractor — plausible overinterpretation of the normal aPTT, but ARUP explicitly includes vitamin K deficiency and liver disease among causes of isolated PT prolongation.
audit_findings.option_D: PASS — directly reproduces the supported differential at the appropriate level of certainty and correctly requires further focused evaluation.
audit_findings.ambiguity: PASS — D is the only option that retains the ARUP-supported differential and the need for further evaluation without asserting an unsupported single cause.
audit_findings.second_answer: EXCLUDED — A assigns the wrong hemostatic mechanism, B overnarrows the differential, and C incorrectly excludes acquired causes.
audit_findings.cueing: PASS — the correct option is no longer uniquely longest; alternatives are clinically parallel and do not rely on a distractor-only absolute-word pattern.
audit_findings.blueprint: PASS — interpreting diagnostic/laboratory results and recognizing the need for focused evaluation align directly with Reduction of Risk Potential.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: PASS — challenged whether B could be accepted because factor VII is the classic isolated-PT factor deficiency and whether liver disease/vitamin K deficiency should require aPTT prolongation. ARUP's current table explicitly lists factor VII deficiency/inhibitor and, in some cases, vitamin K deficiency and liver disease for ↑PT/N aPTT/N platelets. D remains uniquely correct.
